S1.title: WWW-Authenticate header - HTTP | MDN
S1.excerpt:
http

```
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="Staging server", charset="UTF-8" 
```

A user-agent receiving this header would first prompt the user for their username and password, and then re-request the resource with the encoded credentials in the `Authorization` header. The `Authorization` header might look like this:

http

```
Authorization: Basic YWxhZGRpbjpvcGVuc2VzYW1l 
``` [...] A server that supports HOBA authentication might have a `WWW-Authenticate` response header which looks like this:

http

```
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized WWW-Authenticate: HOBA max-age="180", challenge="16:MTEyMzEyMzEyMw==1:028: 
```

The to-be-signed blob challenge is made from these parts: `www.example.com` using port 8080, the nonce is `1123123123`, the algorithm for signing is RSA-SHA256, the key identifier is `123`, and finally the challenge is `68147c97-461b-4310-be9b-4c707237ab53`. [...] A server using HTTP authentication will respond with a `401 Unauthorized` response to a request for a protected resource. This response must include at least one `WWW-Authenticate` header and at least one challenge to indicate what authentication schemes can be used to access the resource and any additional data that each particular scheme needs.

S3.title: WWW-Authenticate - Expert Guide to HTTP headers
S3.excerpt:
A 401 response carries WWW-Authenticate in every case. Responses omitting the header leave browsers with no scheme to satisfy, so no credential prompt appears and the request fails silently. API clients hit the same wall, retrying without knowing which scheme to use. Returning 403 instead communicates a permission problem on valid credentials, which is a different condition. [...] ## Usage

When a client requests a protected resource without valid credentials, the server responds with a 401 status code and includes the WWW-Authenticate header. This header carries one or more authentication challenges, each specifying a scheme and any parameters the client needs to construct valid credentials. [...] # WWW-Authenticate

When a client requests a protected resource without valid credentials, the server needs to communicate which schemes are accepted. The WWW-Authenticate response header carries one or more Authentication challenges alongside a 401 status code.

bundles.question: In HTTP, what does the status code 401 Unauthorized mean according to HTTP semantics standards, including any header/auth expectations (e.g., WWW-Authenticate)?
bundles.summary:
- **Meaning of HTTP 401 Unauthorized (authentication failure semantics):** A `401 Unauthorized` response indicates the target resource **requires authentication**, and the client **has not provided credentials** or provided **invalid/insufficient credentials** for the resource [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/WWW-Authenticate].
- **Authentication challenge expectation (`WWW-Authenticate`):** When issuing a `401`, the server is expected to include **at least one `WWW-Authenticate` header** containing the authentication scheme(s) and scheme-specific challenge parameters so the client can construct an appropriate follow-up request [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/WWW-Authenticate].
- **Scheme-to-header relationship (example behavior):** A `WWW-Authenticate` header causes the client to retry by prompting for/using credentials and sending an `Authorization` header in the follow-up request [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/WWW-Authenticate].
- **Contrast with other status codes (access denial vs auth failure):** Guidance summarized in the sources distinguishes `401` (authentication is required/not satisfied) from `403` (permission problem after valid credentials) [https://http.dev/www-authenticate].
gaps: Direct RFC 9110 normative quotation for the specific `401 Unauthorized` definition was not retrieved in the provided sources; only an RFC-editor pointer to the (now obsolete) RFC 7235 authentication section is available, while the captured normative details about `WWW-Authenticate` come from MDN and a non-RFC explainer [https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7235, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/WWW-Authenticate].

Whether `WWW-Authenticate` is strictly required in *every* 401 case per RFC 9110 text (vs commonly required practice) cannot be confirmed from the provided sources; one external discussion reports real-world cases where 401 is missing `WWW-Authenticate` (but this is not normative RFC text) [https://community.developers.lseg.com/discussion/52787/missing-www-authenticate-header-when-receiving-401-responses].

bundles.question: In HTTP, what does the status code 403 Forbidden mean according to HTTP semantics standards, including any authorization-related expectations?
bundles.summary:
- **HTTP 403 (Forbidden)** means the **server understood the request**, but is **refusing to fulfill it**. [https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html]
- **Authorization-related expectation (per RFC 9110):** if the server receives **valid credentials** that are **not adequate to gain access**, it **ought to respond with 403 (Forbidden)**. [https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html]
- (Conforming summary from a separate source) 403 is described as the server understanding the request but refusing to process it. [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/403]

bundles.question: According to HTTP standards, when should a server return 401 Unauthorized versus 403 Forbidden (e.g., unauthenticated/invalid credentials vs authenticated but insufficient permissions), and how should the server behavior differ between the two?
bundles.summary:
## When to return **401 Unauthorized** vs **403 Forbidden** (HTTP semantics)

### **401 Unauthorized** — authentication required / credentials not yet accepted
- **Meaning:** Use **401** when the client is not authenticated (or the server has not accepted the request’s authentication for access to the protected resource). [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/403] (MDN explains 403, while 401 is described via the authentication challenge flow in the related MDN `WWW-Authenticate` documentation) [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/WWW-Authenticate]
- **Server behavior difference:** A **401 response must include at least one `WWW-Authenticate` header** containing at least one authentication “challenge” describing what authentication schemes and parameters the client can use. [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/WWW-Authenticate]
- **Expected client behavior:** After receiving the `WWW-Authenticate` challenge, the client is expected to retry the request using credentials (typically by sending an `Authorization` header). [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/WWW-Authenticate]

### **403 Forbidden** — authenticated but not permitted for this resource/operation
- **Meaning:** **403** is a client error response where the **server understood the request but refused to process it**, consistent with the idea that the client lacks permission despite understanding/receiving the request. [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/403]
- **Server behavior difference:** Unlike **401**, **403 should not be used as an authentication “challenge” intended to prompt the client to retry with authentication**; the refusal is due to authorization/policy (insufficient permissions). [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/403]

### Registry grounding (RFC references)
- The IANA HTTP Status Code Registry maps **401 Unauthorized** to **RFC9110 Section 15.5.2** and **403 Forbidden** to **RFC9110 Section 15.5.4**. [https://www.iana.org/assignments/http-status-codes]

## Practical mapping (common guidance aligned with the above semantics)
- **401:** “Who are you?” / credentials not accepted yet → challenge and retry with `Authorization`. [https://hyperping.com/blog/401-vs-403-status-codes-whats-the-difference] [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/WWW-Authenticate]
- **403:** “You can’t do that” / permission denied → do not treat as a credentials challenge. [https://hyperping.com/blog/401-vs-403-status-codes-whats-the-difference] [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/403]
gaps: The provided sources do not include the exact RFC 9110 (sections 15.5.2 and 15.5.4) text that explicitly states the 401-vs-403 decision criteria and behavioral requirements; IANA only provides the section mapping, not the detailed RFC wording. [https://www.iana.org/assignments/http-status-codes]

The sources include MDN guidance for `WWW-Authenticate` with 401 and a definition for 403, but the specific statement about what the server should do *not* do in 403 responses (e.g., “do not include `WWW-Authenticate` / do not issue an auth challenge”) is not directly quoted from RFC 9110 in the provided results; it is implied via MDN semantics rather than explicitly evidenced in RFC language. [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/403] [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/WWW-Authenticate]
